items.title: Ken Poston interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 4, 2024
items.q: that might have been him and Coleman Hawkins and Ben Webster and whoever

ctx.x: I could very much speak to that from personal experience in many of these things. It truly is a case by case, band by band kind of a thing. There has to be a leader. Gerry was always very specific and he’s absolutely a thousand percent right, there has to be a leader. So it’s a democratic process when they are actually playing together, because then that role isn’t required. I mean you know then it’s a process where they’re creating music together and everyone has a role that they can take liberties with as…

interpretations. But even for what I do, and I learned very early on of having to put different bands together and create different things. You can’t just usually put a band together and hope that — and say, “Okay we want you to play — we want you to do a tribute to Jazz at the Philharmonic and we want you to do a Jazz at the Philharmonic type concert” because there’ll be a lot of standing around and either one of two things will happen. Either one person that’s a Gerry Mulligan type will just step forward and…

respect from the musicians that they would really, really buckle down when they were doing the rehearsals to show the respect. Sometimes not. Sometimes you would run into problems. But a guy like Gerry, that was never a problem. A guy like Marty Paich was never a problem, because they’re going to get up there, and Gerry didn’t care who it was. When we did those “Rebirth of the Cool” things we did a rehearsal before one of the concerts, that would have been in L.A. at A&M. Herb Alpert would let us use A&M…
